title: Jury rules McPherson's death accidental
article: The family of Larry McPherson praised the three recommendations made by the jury in the coroner's inquest into his death Friday.
The five-member jury ruled the death of the 31-year-old, which occurred after a struggle with police on Aug. 28, 2007, to be an accidental "cocaine-induced sudden death."

The jury called on the RCMP, B.C. Ambulance Service and Office of the Fire Commissioner to ensure all relevant information is communicated to responding emergency service providers before they arrive on a scene, and that personnel are trained in recognizing and responding to people in a state of excited delirium.
The jury also recommended increased funding and resources to raise awareness and provide support to children with learning disabilities, such as McPherson.
"(The jury) couldn't have done much better than that," said Alberta McPherson, Larry's mother, as the recommendations were read.
The victim's sister, Lori McPherson, said the recommendations need to be followed through on to ensure other deaths could be prevented.
Insp. Keith Redl of the Fort St. John RCMP listened to the recommendations and in an interview said his department will review its procedures to see if any areas can be improved.

He said that police are already trained in what is known about excited delirium, a somewhat controversial term used to describe a state of mind characterized by confusion, super-human strength and bizarre behaviour.

However, that recommendation goes against recommendations made in an Independent Review of the Adoption and use of Conducted Energy Weapons conducted for the RCMP, which earlier this year described the condition as "folk knowledge" and recommended deleting it from training manuals.
Redl also said there are times when it is impossible to provide full information to emergency personnel responding to a crisis.
"Communication is difficult when you're running, difficult when you're handling radios and it's difficult when you're trying to restrain someone," he said.

Lori McPherson took the stand Friday to wrap up testimony, telling the inquiry that Larry McPherson's father told him to "scream, yell, break a window and bring attention to yourself" if he was ever being attacked, which may have inadvertently set him on the tragic course.
His father gave him the advice after a group of men broke into his room at the Caravan Hotel, prompting him and a friend to move to the Cedar Lodge.
When someone banged on the window of their room at the Cedar Lodge two days later, Larry McPherson burst out onto the street desperately calling for help.
He ran away from several people he encountered before smashing a squeegee on the window of the Shell station and breaking a window at Deb's Flower Hut.
"He wanted help, but he didn't know what help looked like," said Lori McPherson, who wore a black and white polka-dot blouse and held a tissue.
She began crying from the moment she took the stand on Friday. She praised her brother as a kind-hearted person who struggled through life.

Larry McPherson suffered from developmental disabilities, including Attention Deficit Disorder, and struggled in school as early as Grade 2, at a time when there were few specialists for children with special needs.
At the time of his death, his mother was still in charge of his finances.
He dropped out of school by Grade 8 and found a passion and skill for working with motors, which his sister said he excelled at.
He retreated into himself and became very shy and self-conscious, she said, but he only began using cocaine at about 30 years old, which she suspected was a form of self-medication.
On the night of his death, he had just quit his job at a worksite north of Fort St. John and intended to return home to Terrace, Lori McPherson said. She last spoke to him on the night of Aug. 27.
"He was totally paranoid..." she said. "I just kept telling him 'you got to get on the bus and get home.'"

Dr. Darryl McNaughton, the pathologist who conducted the autopsy, said the many bruises and abrasions that littered his face, knees, legs and arms were "trivial" in nature and couldn't explain his death.
The autopsy didn't reveal anything likely to cause his death other than the amount of cocaine in his blood, McNaughton said.

Toxicologist Dr. Walter Martz testified that at the time of the autopsy Larry McPherson had 10 times the amount of a metabolic byproduct of cocaine known to be potentially fatal, as well as a blood alcohol level of .04 per cent, which may have heightened the effect of the cocaine.
